proposal.proposed_description_short: The ACLU says Project 2025 proposes censoring academic discussions about race, gender and systemic oppression.

proposal.proposed_description_long: The ACLU describes Project 2025 as a federal policy agenda and blueprint for restructuring the executive branch, authored by former Trump administration officials in partnership with the Heritage Foundation. It says the project’s “Mandate for Leadership” is a 900-page manual for reorganizing the federal government agency by agency. Under a section titled “Censoring Critical Discussions in Classrooms,” the ACLU lists a proposal to censor academic discussions about race, gender and systemic oppression. This supports an attributed account of the proposal as the ACLU presents it. The cited explainer does not establish that a federal school ban took effect, identify public schools or other institutions covered by an operative order, or provide the enrollment totals, prosecution record or constitutional ruling asserted in the original entry. Those implementation, scale and legal claims need separate records. The original PEN link returned HTTP 403 in the earlier review; its text is not treated as verified or used here. The revision therefore attributes the proposal to the ACLU and excludes claims that the supplied evidence cannot establish.

proposal.proposed_title: Executive Order 14288 Directs Federal Asset Provision to State and Local Law Enforcement
proposal.proposed_description_short: Executive Order 14288 directs federal agencies to increase provision of excess military and national-security assets to support state and local law enforcement.
proposal.proposed_description_medium: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14288 on April 28, 2025. Section 4(a) directs the Attorney General and Defense Secretary, consulting Homeland Security and other appropriate agencies, to increase provision of excess military and national-security assets in local jurisdictions within 90 days to assist state and local law enforcement. The text is a directive; it does not document completed transfers or their effects.
proposal.proposed_description_long: Executive Order 14288, signed April 28, 2025 and published in the Federal Register on May 2, directs federal officials on law-enforcement resources. Section 4(a) gives the Attorney General and Defense Secretary 90 days to increase the provision of excess military and national-security assets in local jurisdictions to assist state and local law enforcement, after consultation with Homeland Security and appropriate agency heads. Section 4(b) separately tells Defense, in coordination with the Attorney General, to determine how assets, training, non-lethal capabilities and personnel could be used to prevent crime. Section 3(a) calls for federal resources to support law-enforcement practices, training, pay and benefits, legal protections, prison capacity and crime data. Section 3(b) instructs the Attorney General to review ongoing federal consent decrees and related measures, and to modify, rescind or move to conclude measures that unduly impede law-enforcement functions. These provisions document the order’s instructions; they do not show completed asset transfers, particular deployments, effects on policing, a categorical end to consent decrees, or martial law.

proposal.proposed_title: David Pecker Named American Media Chairman and CEO
proposal.proposed_description_short: Variety reported that David Pecker would become chairman and CEO of American Media, the publisher of the National Enquirer, in the 1999 acquisition deal.
proposal.proposed_description_medium: Variety reported on February 16, 1999, that American Media Inc., parent company of the National Enquirer, was being acquired in a deal backed by Evercore Partners and that David Pecker would become American Media’s chairman and CEO. It also said he would receive an equity stake. This does not show that Pecker personally purchased the Enquirer or support describing the publication as “mafia-owned.”
proposal.proposed_description_long: Variety’s February 16, 1999 report described a deal involving American Media Inc., publisher of the National Enquirer and Star. It said David Pecker, then chief executive of Hachette Filipacchi Magazines, was leaving that post to join former Deputy Treasury Secretary Roger Altman’s firm in the acquisition of American Media. The article said Pecker would become American Media’s chairman and CEO and receive an equity stake; it identified Evercore Partners as backing the deal. Variety described the publisher as facing declining earnings and a stagnant stock price after newsstand sales had fallen. It also reported, citing a recent company filing, that National Enquirer and Star sales had declined 12.5 percent over the preceding nine months. These details support an account of a corporate acquisition and Pecker’s executive appointment at the publisher. They do not establish that Pecker personally bought the National Enquirer or support the original “mafia-owned” characterization. The revised account therefore identifies the company transaction and executive role without carrying forward that unsupported ownership claim.

proposal.proposed_title: Massachusetts Court Enjoins Specified Federal Voter-Form Proof Requirements
proposal.proposed_description_short: A 2026 Massachusetts judgment enjoined named federal officials on documentary-proof requirements for specified federal voter-registration forms.
proposal.proposed_description_medium: On July 13, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts entered a permanent injunction concerning Executive Order 14,248. It barred named EAC defendants from requiring documentary citizenship proof on the federal mail voter-registration form and barred the Defense Secretary from adding citizenship or state-eligibility proof to the military and overseas voter postcard form. A separate §4(a) injunction expressly excludes Wisconsin.
proposal.proposed_description_long: On July 13, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts entered a final judgment and permanent injunction in State of California v. Trump, a challenge to Executive Order 14,248. The judgment held plaintiff states other than Wisconsin entitled to summary judgment on §§2(a), 3(d) and 4(a). The injunction’s first clause bars the named Election Assistance Commission defendants from implementing §2(a) or requiring documentary citizenship proof on the federal mail-in voter-registration form. Its second clause bars the Secretary of Defense from implementing §3(d) or altering the federal postcard form used by military and overseas voters to require documentary citizenship proof or proof of eligibility to vote in a particular state. Those two form-specific clauses do not list a narrower group of states in their text. The §4(a) clause separately bars EAC defendants from implementing that section against plaintiff states except Wisconsin, or conditioning specified formula-grant funding on their adoption of §2(a) documentary-proof rules. This proposal follows those distinctions and omits the unsupported appeal claim; the cited judgment and opinion do not establish a later appeal filing or appellate outcome.

proposal.proposed_title: Interior Approved ANWR Leasing; BLM Held the First Sale and Issued Nine Leases
proposal.proposed_description_short: Interior approved an ANWR Coastal Plain leasing program in 2020; BLM held the first sale in 2021 and issued nine leases covering 437,804 acres.
proposal.proposed_description_medium: The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act required a Coastal Plain leasing program in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, and Interior approved its program in August 2020. BLM’s January 2021 sale received 13 bids totaling $14,412,458; the agency later issued leases for nine tracts covering 437,804 acres. The releases describe approvals, bids and leases, not drilling; further ground action required additional environmental analysis.
proposal.proposed_description_long: The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act required Interior to establish a leasing program on the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge’s Coastal Plain. Interior signed the program record of decision on August 17, 2020, specifying where and under what terms leasing could occur on the 1.56-million-acre Coastal Plain. BLM held the first sale on January 6, 2021. It received 13 bids totaling $14,412,458; the agency said bids covered 552,802 acres and it had offered 22 tracts, withdrawing 10 after comments from Alaska Native tribes, conservation organizations and the Canadian government. On January 19, BLM announced that leases had been issued for nine tracts covering 437,804 acres. The releases document program approval, bids and issued leases. They do not establish that wells were drilled or production began. BLM said any further action on the ground would require additional environmental analysis. The entry should describe a leasing program and lease sale, not assert drilling was opened or started, environmental damage occurred, or lobbying caused the decision.
